title: Modi and Macron Have Drawn Up a Five-Year Plan to Double Trade. Here Is Everything They Agreed at Villa Kerylos.
excerpt: An Innovation Roadmap 2030, a joint AI working group, a new dialogue on critical minerals, and 19 signed agreements — the Nice summit delivered substance, not just ceremony.
body:
Modi and Macron met at Villa Kerylos, a Belle Époque landmark perched above the Mediterranean in Nice, for talks that covered everything from fighter jets to French university campuses in India. It was their first sit-down since the bilateral relationship was elevated to a 'Special Global Strategic Partnership' in February — and the agenda matched the title.

The centrepiece was a new Innovation Roadmap 2030, a formal framework to give the technology partnership a long-term direction. Alongside it, the two leaders announced a Joint India-France AI Working Group to deepen cooperation in artificial intelligence — a sector where both countries see an opportunity to set norms rather than follow them.

On trade, they agreed to establish a high-level mechanism to double bilateral trade within five years, a target that would push the annual figure past $30 billion. Both leaders called for the early implementation of the India-EU Free Trade Agreement, which has been under negotiation for over a decade and would unlock preferential access for Indian goods across all 27 EU member states.

"On trade, they agreed to establish a high-level mechanism to double bilateral trade within five years, a target that would push the annual figure past $30 billion."

A new Economic Security Dialogue was announced to strengthen supply chain resilience in critical minerals — the raw materials that underpin everything from electric vehicles to semiconductors. France, which controls significant nickel and cobalt reserves through its overseas territories, is a natural partner for India's push to de-risk its mineral imports from China.

!Villa Kerylos — Photo: Wikimedia Commons

In defence, the two sides agreed to intensify co-design, co-development and co-production of platforms and advanced technologies. India is already one of the largest operators of French Rafale jets and Scorpène submarines; the expanded collaboration could bring more manufacturing to Indian soil under the 'Make in India' initiative. France is already India's second-largest defence supplier after Russia, and the expanded framework could accelerate discussions on additional Rafale orders, Safran jet engine technology transfer, and joint production of naval systems. They also discussed deepening cooperation in human spaceflight and space situational awareness, building on ISRO's Gaganyaan programme and France's extensive launch infrastructure through CNES, its national space agency. The collaboration could extend to India's planned space station and future lunar missions.

Nuclear energy featured prominently. India's recently enacted SHANTI Act — which overhauls the country's civil nuclear liability framework — was described as opening new doors for collaboration, particularly on small and advanced modular reactors. France's EDF and India's NPCIL have long discussed large reactor projects at Jaitapur, Maharashtra, but the modular route could prove faster and more commercially viable.

On people-to-people ties, Macron's government has operationalised visa-free transit for Indian nationals at French airports — a practical win for the nearly two million Indians who transit through Paris each year. Modi invited French universities to open campuses in India under the New Education Policy, and both sides agreed to expand mutual recognition of educational qualifications. The move would make it easier for Indian graduates to work in France and vice versa — a significant benefit for the estimated 50,000 Indian students currently enrolled in French universities.

The innovation conclave also produced 19 signed agreements between Indian and French institutions across deep-tech, semiconductors, agri-tech, med-tech, renewable energy, and space.

For the Indian diaspora in Europe, the outcomes signal a partnership that is moving beyond defence deals and diplomatic statements into territory that directly affects visas, education, trade access and technology transfer. The Innovation Roadmap 2030, if executed, could make France the anchor of India's European strategy in the same way Japan has become its anchor in Asia.

Modi heads to Bratislava next for a historic state visit to Slovakia — the first by an Indian Prime Minister since Slovak independence in 1993 — before returning to France for the G7 Summit in Évian, where a closely watched bilateral with Trump awaits.
